It links the daemon's own `treecopy_recursive()` rather than growing a fourth tree-copy — that one already reports *which* entry stopped it, the difference between a diagnosable install failure and a bare `No such file or directory`. Both halves are confirmed to run: the ISO build logs `staged the package seed from ...` and the installer logs `cix-install: staged the package seed`. A first boot now also reports its own progress on the console (`default image: no C library -- installing glibc`, then `default image: ready`), which is right for a fresh install regardless of tests — the log store is not reachable that early. **What is not yet true:** on a real installed box neither console marker appears, so the daemon is not reaching the seed there, while a locally-run daemon against an identically-shaped data directory installs it correctly every time. That is a difference in the installed environment, not a timing problem — it was still absent with the boot budget raised to 600s. `test_installer` is left **failing on purpose** rather than adjusted to pass: it is correctly reporting that a freshly installed host still cannot run a container, which is the whole point of #189.

- **And it verifies those bytes, because the cache is about to gain a writer it never had.** A cache hit deliberately skips fetching *and* verifying — the fetch child exits immediately and the install stages straight from the cache. That is sound only because of an invariant: everything in that cache was verified on the way **in**, either a download checked against `pkg_artifact_sha256` or an artifact this host built itself. The installer seed (#189 part 2) will be the first thing to write that directory before the daemon has ever run, so the seed path re-verifies the cached artifact against its own recipe before installing it — keeping the invariant true rather than widening the daemon's trust to whatever wrote its cache. The artifact server was never a trust boundary; neither is install media. Proven by flipping one byte of a cached artifact and starting a real daemon against it: *"the cached glibc@2.44-6 artifact is not the bytes its own recipe approves -- refusing to install it."*

- **A fresh box gives its own default image a C library, through the package pipeline (#189, part 1).** Closing the glibc floor left `ensure_default_image()` creating `base` with the ordinary baseline — which no longer carries a runtime borrowed from the build host. Correct, but it left the one image a fresh install actually has unable to run anything, which `test_installer` caught on a real QEMU install-and-boot. The daemon now installs a C library into the default image when it has none, at startup, through `pkg_install_start()` like any other install — so the image ends up with a real manifest entry, a version and an upgrade path, **never a copy**, which is the distinction ADR-0216 exists to hold. It refuses unless the artifact is already cached: a recipe alone is not enough, because building glibc on a box with no toolchain is a long failure rather than a fix, and the container-create guard already tells an operator exactly what to install. Same best-effort, never-block-startup posture as the kmsg and uevent watches beside it, and a silent no-op on every boot after the first. The loader path that answers "can this image run anything" is now defined once (`PKG_IMAGE_LOADER_REL`) instead of written out separately in three places that must not drift. `test_pkg` proves it by **removing** its own explicit glibc install and asserting the daemon did it instead — through the package manifest and its version, not by looking for the file, since arriving as a versioned package rather than a copy is the whole point. Disabling the seed fails that assertion, and the reintroduction also caught the assertion printing an uninitialised buffer when no state was ever reported — fixed, because a diagnostic that prints garbage is the thing this project keeps having to fix.

- **Audit: a documented endpoint that was not in the contract, and five ADR links pointing at the wrong decisions.** `GET /v1/system/kmsg` — the kernel ring buffer, and the only way to read dmesg on a host that deliberately has no shell — has been served since ADR-0179 phase 2c and appeared nowhere in `openapi.yaml`, which the Documentation Map names as *the* authoritative REST contract. Now declared there and described in `docs/api/README.md` in the same change, per the rule that exists because those two drifted ten phases apart once already. Separately, five ADR cross-links resolved to nothing: three named a real ADR by a filename it never had, and two were worse — ADR-0207 claimed to supersede "the OverlayFS shared-lower storage model (ADR-0079, ADR-0080)", but ADR-0079 is cgroup controller delegation and ADR-0080 is container diagnostics visibility. Neither has anything to do with overlay storage; the model it actually supersedes is ADR-0004. Corrected in place, which the ADR process permits for a factual error as distinct from reversing a decision. Every ADR *number* cited across the whole tree does resolve to a real ADR — only these five paths were wrong — and there are now zero broken internal links in any markdown file.

- **The no-C-library refusal named garbage instead of the image.** Found by running the new guard on a real box rather than trusting the test: it formatted its message after `json_free(root)`, and `image` points into that tree, so a real host reported ``image "<garbage bytes>" has no C library``. A diagnostic whose entire purpose is to save someone from an opaque exit 127 is worth nothing if it cannot say which image it means. Looking for the same shape found two more, both pre-existing: `"no such volume: %s"` and `"could not resolve volume %s"` both read `vname` after the tree holding it was freed. (The bridged-network refusal nearby looks identical but formats from a local buffer and is fine.) `test_images` now asserts the refusal *names the image*, not merely that it is a 400 — putting the free back reproduces the garbage and fails it.

- **The glibc floor is closed: nothing in any image is copied off the build host any more (#186, ADR-0216).** The four files `pkg_seed_image_baseline()` borrowed by absolute path — the loader (twice), libc, libm and the files-NSS backend — are gone. They were the last bytes in the system this project did not build, and ADR-0209 said closing them meant building glibc from source on a Cix host; that is done, so an image gets its C library by installing a package, with a version and an auditable origin, like everything else. A freshly created image therefore has no runtime, which is correct rather than a gap — `POST /v1/containers` refuses one and names what to install. `test_images` now asserts the **inverse** of what it asserted before, and was proven to catch the regression by restoring the copies from the previous commit: *"something is copying one off the build host again."* Three test images that run containers (`router`, `pintest`, `rollctrimg`) now install glibc, which is the point rather than a chore — the guarantee those tests always made, that a binary in an image can actually `execve`, is now earned by a package instead of granted by a copy. On 192.168.15.95 every image took glibc as a cache hit needing no build environment, and a container from the resulting version ran a real dynamically-linked binary to a clean exit 0.

- **A composed build environment gets this platform's own C library, and is checked for it (#186, steps 1–2).** The environment holds exactly its declared tools' manifest files, and no tool's manifest carries libc — so until now the loader in it arrived only because `pkg_seed_image_baseline()` copied one off whatever distribution the build host runs. `glibc` is now an implicit member of every composed environment, resolved through the same `buildenv_add_tool()` path as any declared tool: declared tools are resolved first and dedup is by name, so a recipe keeps the right to pin `glibc@2.44-6`. Named once in `PKG_BASE_LIBC` rather than written into sixty recipes, because every binary in every package links against libc — that is a property of an environment being usable, not of any one recipe, and sixty declarations would be sixty chances to omit it, each failing only at exec time. Because an environment's identity is the sorted tool-set hash, every environment composed under the old rule retires by construction and the next build re-composes with glibc inside; no staleness is possible. **And it is verified, not trusted:** composition copies tools in sorted name order, so a tool sorting after `glibc` that ships a path glibc owns would silently win it, and glibc's objects share a version-locked private interface — halves of two C libraries cannot exec. `buildenv_verify_libc_intact()` re-reads the loader and `libc.so.6` before the environment is sealed and refuses one whose copies are not byte-identical to what the glibc package installed. That is the discipline `mkbootroot` earned this week, for the same reason. `test_pkg` stages the collision deliberately — a `zzlibc` package shipping its own `libc.so.6`, declared as a build tool, isolated in its own image so it cannot corrupt `base` — and asserts composition refuses. Measured with the gate removed, which is the argument for having it: the build still fails, but as `build failed (exit 127)`, the opaque broken-loader exit that names no file, package, or cause. The glibc artifact's `pkg_artifact_sha256` is recorded from bytes 192.168.15.95 built with our own gcc and published; it joins the ADR-0209 test floor. The four host copies are still in place — this step deliberately lands while they are, so environments are proven self-sufficient before anything is removed.

- **A container cannot be created from an image with no C library, and now says so.** Groundwork for #186, which closes ADR-0209's "glibc floor" — the four glibc files still copied off the build host into every image, the last bytes in the system this project did not build. Those copies are what makes an image *always* have a runtime today, so this check is inert; it is in place ahead of the migration that makes an image without one a reachable state. It looks for the dynamic loader rather than for a package named glibc, because the requirement is a working runtime and which package provides it belongs to the catalogue, not the daemon. Without it the failure surfaces much later as a container exiting 127 with `execve failed`, which describes the symptom and names nothing. The image-GC fixture now stages a loader alongside its fabricated binaries, since the versions it invents stand in for real images.

- **A hostbuild's file list grew by its whole contents on every rebuild (#185).** `cix` reported its twelve files five times over. A hostbuild *merges* into its artifact directory rather than replacing it, and the ordinary install path has always forgotten the previous file list before `merge_tree()` repopulates it — the hostbuild branch, added later for reporting alone, never picked that reset up, so each round appended. Five entries because `cix` had gone rc24 → rc28 through one package entry; it would have kept growing. The paths on disk were always correct — only the record of them was wrong, which is why nothing broke visibly, while `pkg delete`'s ownership check (#175) re-asked the same question once per duplicate. One line, plus a test that upgrades a hostbuild to a second version and asserts the count is **unchanged** rather than merely non-empty: the broken version reported a perfectly plausible non-empty list. Backing the line out fails that check with `1 -> 2`.

- **Everything this platform actually builds for itself was silently unpublishable to the artifact cache.** The question that found it was a fair one: why is `cix` not in the cache, and no kernel either? Two defects, and the reason neither was obvious is that ordinary source-built packages publish themselves automatically at build time, so the cache looked like proof the mechanism worked — `glibc` and `gawk` were both sitting in it. Every package that was *missing* turned out to be a hostbuild. First: a hostbuild's artifact is a **directory** this host assembled, never a tarball it fetched, so nothing ever put one in the local cache that `pkg_artifact_push_try_start()` reads from, and the push had nothing to send. Second: `POST /v1/pkg/{name}/artifact/publish` only *enqueued*, and nothing pumps that queue except a completing build — the endpoint answered `202 {"status":"queued"}` and then sat there indefinitely, which is exactly what it did for `cix`, `kernel` and `isotools`, with not one line in the log saying so. Publishing on request now schedules its own work like every other caller of the pump, and when the tarball is missing the publish first builds one from the installed tree using the same export that already guarantees byte-identical output across hosts (ADR-0201) — landing it directly at the cache path a push reads, so there is one tarball in one place rather than a second parallel route to the cache. `test_pkg_cache` now builds a real hostbuild and asserts its artifact **arrives at the receiving server**, deliberately not that the request was accepted, since `202` is precisely what the broken endpoint returned. Confirmed to fail on exactly those two checks and nothing else when the fix is backed out. The build_image fixture both pkg tests need moved into `test_image_fixture.c` rather than being copied, so the ADR-0107/0108 image layout has one definition in the suite instead of two that drift.

- **The build host's C library was overwriting the one this platform builds, and assembly reported success every time.** `mkbootroot` stages the platform's own glibc — the 2.44 set built on a Cix host — into the control-plane root. It staged it *early*, right after `cixd`. The host-sourced library list (`shelled_bin_libs`) runs later, and it names `libm.so.6`, `libpthread.so.0` and `libresolv.so.2`, which are glibc's own objects: the build host's 2.36 copies landed on top of ours, every single time. Those objects share a private, version-locked interface with `libc.so.6`, so the root shipped mismatched halves of one library — init exits 127 and the kernel panics on `Attempted to kill init!`. Two boot failures on .95 came from this, and neither assembly ever printed a warning, because copying files is not the same as producing a root that runs. The staging now happens last, after every host-sourced copy, so the platform's own libraries are the final word. Ordering alone was not accepted as the fix: right before the image is sealed, `verify_platform_libs_intact()` re-reads every platform library and refuses to write an image whose root no longer carries the exact bytes the platform built, naming the file that was replaced. Confirmed by putting the original ordering back — the gate stops the build at `libpthread.so.0` and no squashfs is produced — and by chrooting into a root assembled from the real `cix` artifact, where the same `cixd` that panicked now loads and runs. Part of the #181 work to stop borrowing a foreign libc at all.

- **`cix-install` rejects an argument it does not recognise, instead of ignoring it.** Found while making ADR-0213's "a stale `--auto-partition` now fails loudly" claim actually true: the argument loop had no final `else`, so anything unknown was silently dropped. `--auto-partition` was the harmless case. A mistyped `--skip-partiton` was not — it would have been discarded, leaving the installer to partition and destroy a disk the operator was explicitly trying to preserve, with no diagnostic anywhere. The flag whose typo costs the most was the one with no protection at all. Unknown arguments are now fatal and name the offender; a bare `--` is tolerated, since whether the kernel passes the separator through to init's argv is the bootloader's business.

- **The isotools path layout keeps the dev fallback working (`isotools 2.14-5`).** `mkinstalleriso` resolves the harvested tools as `<isotools-root>/...`, and `<isotools-root>` is a plain `/usr` for a bare development-machine invocation — that is precisely how the tool keeps working off a Cix host. Staging `fdisk`/`mkfs.fat` under `bin/` by analogy with `mokutil` made those resolve to `/usr/bin/fdisk`, which exists on no Debian box: the Cix path would have kept working while the dev path silently broke. They move to `sbin/`, matching where a development machine really keeps them.

- **The installer image's library closure is derived from the binaries, not maintained by hand — and the dev path builds a real fixture instead of pretending `/usr` is an artifact.** `mkinstalleriso` carried two hardcoded closure arrays, one per source tree, and neither could have been right: a single list cannot describe two different sets of binaries, and these are two different sets. Debian's `mkfs.btrfs` needs `libudev.so.1` and ours does not; ours links `libz.so.1` and Debian's does not; Debian keeps libcrypt's obsolete DES/NIS ABI at soname `.so.1` while our libxcrypt drops it and ships `.so.2`. Every correction made for one host broke the other, and it broke *quietly* — the ISO built fine and the installer died at exec time inside a QEMU boot with `mkfs.btrfs failed (status 0x7f00)`. Both lists are gone. `test_image_fixture_stage_closure()` reads a binary's real ELF `DT_NEEDED` entries and follows them transitively, resolving each SONAME against the tree that binary came from — this machine's library directories for a host tool, the isotools artifact's own for one taken out of it. A library that cannot be resolved is a hard error naming both the library and the binary that wanted it, so the failure lands at ISO-build time instead of at install time. `libc.so.6` and the loader are deliberately never re-staged, since `test_image_fixture_build()` has already put a matching runtime in place. The claim that passing a plain `"/usr"` "reproduces the tool's original host-borrowed behaviour" had expired silently the moment the tool started reading Cix-built binaries, and `test_installer` had not been run since, so nobody noticed; it now builds a real isotools-root fixture from this machine's own tools in the artifact's exact layout. A fixture is honest about being a stand-in. **`test_installer` passes end to end again** — ISO assembly, scripted partitioning, btrfs format, payload write, MOK enrolment, Secure Boot verification and a running `cixd` across two independent boots.

- **Removing a package no longer deletes files another package owns (#175).** Two packages legitimately owning one path is ordinary — glibc and linux-headers both own parts of `usr/include`, and any two packages built from a shared upstream tree overlap — and whichever installed last is what is on disk. Uninstall removed every path in a manifest regardless, so the *survivor* was left reported as installed, with a recorded manifest, and its files gone. Nothing failed at the time. This is not hypothetical: uninstalling `libc-dev` to make way for the self-built glibc silently gutted `linux-headers`, and the damage surfaced later and elsewhere as `copying usr/include/asm-generic/resource.h from declared tool linux-headers@6.18.40-4 (image cix-builder) failed: No such file or directory` — a build environment that could no longer be composed, blamed on a package nobody had touched. Removal now skips any path another installed package in the same image also claims, and reports how many it kept. Leaving a shared file behind is the conservative direction deliberately: it demonstrably belongs to something still installed, so keeping it costs disk, while deleting it breaks a package that was never touched, far from the cause. Ownership is scoped per image, since that is the unit a manifest describes. `test_pkg` installs two packages sharing a path, deletes one, and asserts both the survivor's own file and the shared file remain — while still asserting the deleted package's *unshared* file is gone, so the fix cannot degrade into a no-op. Confirmed to fail without the fix with exactly the message it was written for.

- **An image whose current version predated the btrfs migration could never be installed into again — or uninstalled from, or deleted (#180).** Every `pkg install` into `cix-builder` on .95 failed with a message blaming the package (`zlib failed to merge installed files into the target image`) while the daemon log said what actually happened: `image cix-builder: could not produce a new version -- snapshotting the current rootfs forward failed: Invalid argument`. `EINVAL` from `BTRFS_IOC_SNAP_CREATE_V2` means **the source is not a subvolume**: the ADR-0207 phase 4 storage migration copies content faithfully, which turns subvolumes into ordinary directories, and nothing notices until the next snapshot. The image was then completely frozen, because uninstall goes through the same call and `DELETE /v1/images` refuses while packages remain — a condition that cannot be satisfied. That is also a bootstrap trap: repairing it needs a new `cixd`, building `cixd` needs a working build image. `cix_btrfs_snapshot_or_copy()` now tests whether the source really is a subvolume (inode 256, `BTRFS_FIRST_FREE_OBJECTID` — the same test btrfs-progs uses) and, when it is not, creates the destination as a real subvolume and copies into it. One full copy, once, after which the image's current version *is* a subvolume and every later version snapshots in O(1) as intended — it repairs itself by being used. The reporting is fixed too: the failure names the image and what it could not do rather than an innocent package, the same discipline `childdiag.c` exists for.

- **The `cix` artifact stops shipping 21 MB of build output (#178).** Observed in the artifact cache: `cix` was **561 KB** at v2.1.1 and **22.8 MB** at v2.2.0-rc6, while the package's own files — `cixd`, `cixctl`, `mkbootroot`, `cix-install`, `cix-recover`, `mkinstalleriso`, `web/` — total about 1.5 MB. `spawn_cix_bootroot_assembly()` wrote both of its paths *inside the artifact directory*: the assembled `cixd-root.squashfs` (~10 MB) and `.bootroot-stage/` (~12 MB, an uncompressed copy of the tree that squashfs was built from). The staging tree was never cleaned up — the string appeared exactly once in the whole codebase, on the line that created it — and export tars the whole directory, so both were published. Every host pulling `cix` downloaded ~22 MB to use 1.5 MB of it, plus a stale squashfs it would never read. Both now live in `REBUILDABLE_DIR/bootroot/`, a sibling of `artifacts/` and `iso/`; the staging tree is removed when the assembly child is reaped, on success and failure alike. Because a hostbuild *merges* into the artifact directory rather than replacing it, the daemon also clears the old files once at startup — not a compatibility shim, just finishing the move, since they were never package content and nothing reads them there any more. The path moving broke one real contract: `cixctl pkg hostbuild cix --deploy` composed `<artifact_path>/cixd-root.squashfs` itself (ADR-0057). It now reads a new `bootroot_image_path` from `GET /system/boot` — the same response it already polls for the assembly generation — which is also more API-First than before, since the CLI stops knowing a server-side filesystem layout at all.

- **There is no interactive partitioning any more (ADR-0214, superseding ADR-0213 the same day).** ADR-0213 made the scripted layout the default — that stands — but kept the interactive `fdisk` session behind `--interactive`, on two arguments that did not survive being checked against the code. The first: "the installer media carries no shell, so `fdisk` is the only escape hatch." True premise (there is no `/bin/sh`, no busybox, and `cix-recover` contains no `execve` at all) and a false conclusion — `find_partition_device()` requires five exactly-named GPT partitions, so the *structure* is fixed no matter who writes the table, and an interactive session could only ever vary four **sizes**. Of those, `cix-containers` is already better served by growing into the space ADR-0190 deliberately leaves unallocated, over the REST API, in the reversible direction; the other three are platform constants (the control-plane squashfs is ~10 MB against a 160 MiB root slot — 16× headroom) that would be wrong for every install or none, and whose fix is the constant, not an operator's typing. The second argument — "we would lose `test_installer`'s QEMU-driven `fdisk` session, which already caught a real shipped bug" — is circular: it keeps a feature in order to keep the test *of that feature*. The test was evidence the path worked, never that it was needed. So `--interactive` is gone, `recipes/package/fdisk/` is deleted, `isotools` no longer harvests it, `mkinstalleriso` no longer stages it, and the interactive walkthrough is out of `installing.md`. `--skip-partition` remains for a disk prepared elsewhere. `sfdisk` was never in question — it does all the real partition work here and comes off the control-plane root, where it already lives for `cixd`'s own partition management.

- **Scripted partitioning is the install default now (ADR-0213).** `cix-install` used to drop into an interactive `fdisk` session when given no flag, with the scripted layout behind `--auto-partition`. That is backwards, and not for convenience reasons: the installer reads partition *roles* back from GPT partition **names**, so an operator driving `fdisk` by hand has to reproduce `cix-esp`/`cix-root-a`/`cix-root-b`/`cix-config`/`cix-containers` byte-for-byte, in order, with the right types — a contract `fdisk`'s own interface says nothing about, and whose violation surfaces much later as a partition role that cannot be found. The error-prone path was the one you fell into by default. ADR-0190 had already made the scripted layout adaptive (real disk size from sysfs, `cix-containers` capped, remainder deliberately unallocated) and a running host partitions that remainder over REST, so the usual reason to want a manual editor is now answered after install rather than during it. `--auto-partition` is **removed**, not kept as a no-op alias — a flag retained only so old invocations keep working is the legacy shim this project does not carry, and an invocation still passing it now fails with a usage error rather than quietly meaning something else. The interactive path stays behind an explicit `--interactive`: deleting it was considered and rejected on one fact — the installer media carries no shell at all, so without `fdisk` a machine the standard layout does not suit could not be partitioned from the ISO at all, and `test_installer.c`'s QEMU-driven `fdisk` session (which already caught one real shipped bug, `cfdisk`'s unstaged terminfo) would have gone with it.

- **One rule for which line of a failed child's output an operator sees (`daemon/src/childdiag.c`).** The question was answered twice, in two files, and each answer was wrong in the case the other one handled. `diskformat.c` preferred the last line opening a diagnostic, because `mkfs.btrfs` ends a failure with a documentation-URL footer. The ISO assembly took the literal last line — and paid for it live: `mkinstalleriso` closes a failure with its own summary of which tool exited nonzero, one line *below* the reason that tool printed, so the operator got `.../isotools/bin/sbsign failed (status 0x100)` while the actual cause (`Error reading file .../systemd-bootx64.efi: No such file or directory`) was recoverable only from the log store. Both call sites now use one helper: the last line opening an error marker, else the last non-empty line, matched case-insensitively — which matters, because the earlier matcher compared `ERROR` and `error` only and the spelling that mattered was `Error`. `test_childdiag` asserts both real captures verbatim, and was confirmed to fail on all of them when the old rule is put back.

- **The ISO build clears every host input but one, and it is now tracked (#177).** With the above, `POST /system/iso` on .95 stages all five installer tools and the full library closure and reaches the Secure Boot signing step, where it stops on `systemd-bootx64.efi` — an absolute path into a Debian systemd install, staged into the ISO so `cix-install` can write it to the target ESP. Every absolute path `mkinstalleriso` reads has now been enumerated against `mkbootroot.c`'s staged-binary list, so this is known to be the last one rather than the next one: `sfdisk`/`mkfs.ext4`/`mkfs.btrfs` and the nine libraries are on a Cix root; `fdisk`/`mkfs.fat`/shim/MokManager/`mokutil` are packages harvested into isotools; only sd-boot has no source. Packaging it needs meson and ninja, neither of which exists yet.

- **The installer's own tools now come from packages, and the closure was wrong in both directions.** With the output capture in place, the next ISO build named its cause exactly — `/usr/sbin/fdisk: No such file or directory` — instead of another bare exit status. Rather than fix that one path and rediscover the next, every absolute path `mkinstalleriso` reads was checked against `mkbootroot.c`'s own staged-binary list, which is authoritative because a control-plane root is built from it. Three were wrong, in three different ways: `fdisk` and `mkfs.fat` are genuinely absent and rightly so (cixd never partitions interactively and never formats FAT, so that root has no reason to carry either) — both are packages now, `fdisk 2.42.2-4` and `dosfstools 4.2-1`, harvested into the isotools artifact alongside shim and mokutil; `mke2fs` was present under a different name, since `mkfs.ext4` is a link to it on Debian but a Cix root has only the `mkfs.ext4` name that `DISKFORMAT_MKFS_EXT4_BIN` uses. The library closure had errors pointing opposite ways: `libudev.so.1` was staged and is gone (no Cix root has it, yet .95 formats disks with both `mkfs.ext4` and `mkfs.btrfs` from that root, so the Cix-built binaries demonstrably do not need it), and `libz.so.1` was missing and is now staged — `mkfs.btrfs` links zlib unconditionally, and its absence would not have failed an ISO *build* at all, only produced an installer whose `mkfs.btrfs` could not start, discovered at install time, on the filesystem ADR-0207 phase 4 makes the default. Both new recipes assert their real `DT_NEEDED` against the built ELF rather than trusting a configure flag, so "it needs nothing but libc" is measured, not claimed. `fdisk` took four revisions and every one of them was an already-documented trap re-encountered: `--disable-all-programs --enable-fdisk` is advertised in configure's help text with no `AC_ARG_ENABLE` behind it (getopt 2.42.2-2 documents this; -1 grepped configure for the option string, which finds the help text, not the registration), libsmartcols hits TCC's glibc `<regex.h>` gap, and finally `__builtin_clz` — issue #176, the same TCC defect that shipped a broken libblkid, here caught loudly at link time because an executable's link fails on an undefined symbol where a shared library's does not. Resolved the way libblkid already resolved it, Tier 3 with gcc, rather than inventing a second answer to a defect this project has answered once.

- **`POST /system/iso` cannot work on a Cix host, and the signing keys were only the first of eight walls.** With ADR-0212's key pair installed, the ISO build got past every precondition and then failed with `mkinstalleriso failed (status 0x100)` — an exit status and nothing else, because the child's stdout and stderr went to a pipe nobody created. That is the **third** time this exact gap has cost a cycle (#125, #132, and the artifact-export stderr fix), so it is now closed properly: `mkinstalleriso`'s output is captured, drained incrementally through its own epoll conn (grub-mkrescue and mksquashfs are chatty enough to fill a 64K pipe, and a full pipe would hang the child rather than fail it), logged, and its **last line is appended to the error `GET /system/iso` reports** — the field an operator actually reads. The bootroot capture was generalised into a shared `struct child_output` rather than copied, since a second set of module globals doing the same thing is exactly what "no parallel implementations" rules out. **The cause was then found statically rather than by another deploy round**: `mkinstalleriso` stages seven things a Cix control-plane root simply does not have — `/usr/bin/mokutil`, `/usr/lib/shim/shimx64.efi.signed`, `/usr/lib/shim/mmx64.efi.signed`, and `libcrypt.so.1`, `libdl.so.2`, `libefivar.so.1`, `libudev.so.1` — none of which `mkbootroot` stages. All seven are present on the development machine, which is precisely why every ISO to date was built there and none on a box. shim and MokManager are Microsoft-signed Debian binaries that Cix cannot produce by design (ADR-0015), so how they reach a host is a real decision, not a bug to patch.
- **The kernel on 192.168.15.95 was built on the dev machine, and the recipe that did it lives only on the box.** `kernel 6.18.40-16` is not in this repository. Its own comment states plainly what it is: *"192.168.15.95 has no gcc-bearing dev build image (its kernels have always come from the dev-machine build), so the btrfs kernel was built on the dev machine ... and published to the artifact cache; this line lets `pkg hostbuild kernel` on the box take the artifact tier and skip the on-box build it cannot run."* A kernel compiled with a foreign toolchain, published to the cache and booted — what the Build Provenance Mandate rules out in as many words. It also kept a real bug invisible: because nothing on the box ever ran `pkg_build()`, nobody noticed the recipe wrote its `syslimits.h` correction to a **hardcoded** `.../12.5.0/include-fixed/` path, the gcc that happened to be installed when it was written. `elfutils 0.192-8` had already fixed exactly this, for exactly this correction, against exactly this gcc install; the kernel recipe was simply never updated to match. **`6.18.40-17` approves no artifact at all** — the kernel is built on a Cix host or it is not shipped — and asks gcc its own version. The premise behind `-16` is gone: `kernel-builder` now exists and holds a real gcc toolchain.
- **`kernel-builder` took three rounds to become buildable, each one read rather than guessed.** `1.0.1` moved two pins that named versions absent from the cache. `1.0.2` moved gawk from `5.3.0-2` to `5.3.0-7` after the build reached code generation and died on `awk: error while loading shared libraries: libtinfo.so.6` — `DT_NEEDED` read off both published artifacts settled it (`-2` pulls `libreadline.so.8`, hence libtinfo; `-7` needs only libc and libm), and the whole image was then swept the same way, every binary of every installed package against what the image provides, with libtinfo the only real gap. `1.0.3` added `findutils`, `gzip` and `diffutils` after `xargs: command not found` killed **every** archive step (`cmd_ar_builtin` builds `built-in.a` in every directory). Rather than add xargs and rediscover the next one a build at a time, the kernel's own build machinery was read — the top-level Makefile, `Makefile.build`, `Makefile.lib`, `link-vmlinux.sh` and arch/x86's Makefiles — which also established what is **not** needed: perl is reached only through `recordmcount.pl` (ftrace, off under allnoconfig), and python3, rsync, patch, zstd and bc are not on the `bzImage` path at all.
- **Decontaminating `libc-dev` broke cix's own build, which is the clearest measure of how much the contamination was hiding.** `cixd` has linked `-lssl -lcrypto` and included `<openssl/ssl.h>` since Phase 9, and `cix.recipe` never declared openssl — it built because `libc-dev 2.36-5`'s `cp -a /usr/include/.` delivered OpenSSL's headers as a side effect of a package with nothing to do with OpenSSL. With `2.36-8` staging 106 named glibc headers and nothing else, that side effect is gone. Caught before a failed build rather than by one: every non-glibc system header included anywhere in this repository was swept, and `openssl/{ssl,bio,err,pem}.h` are the only ones — so declaring openssl is the whole correction, not the first instalment of it.
- **A signing key pair can finally reach a host at all (ADR-0212).** `POST /v1/system/iso` has required a Secure Boot key pair at `<data-dir>/keys/` since ADR-0064, which called it an operator-populated-out-of-band precondition and compared it to a file already `scp`'d onto the box. That comparison was the defect: a real Cix host runs **no sshd** (port 22 refused), exposes no host-side exec route (every `/v1/system/*` path was enumerated — `boot-console` is GET/PUT config, not a shell), and has no console. There was no band to be out of, so **that endpoint has never been servable on any real installed host** — a required input with no supported way to supply it, shipped complete with a CLI command and a guide that could not run. New `GET`/`PUT`/`DELETE /v1/system/signing-keys` takes the pair as two PEM blocks. ADR-0064's actual security property is untouched — cixd still never generates, fetches or copies the key on its own initiative, and only the public DER `.cer` reaches an installed target — and neither half of this is new ground here: `pkg_repo_set_config()` already accepts the git token over REST and reports `auth_token_set` rather than the token, and `pki.c` has always generated and stored private keys under `STATE_DIR/pki`. **The key goes in and never comes back**: GET reports two booleans plus the certificate's own subject/expiry/SHA-256 fingerprint, and the test asserts against the raw response body that no field ever echoes key material. The DER `.cer` is **derived** from the certificate rather than accepted separately (proven byte-identical to `openssl x509 -outform DER`), because two independently supplied encodings can disagree and the failure that produces is an enrolled MOK identity that doesn't match what signed the image. The pair is verified to match **before anything is written** and the write is atomic: a mismatched paste is the realistic mistake a copy-paste interface enables, both blobs parse individually so nothing else would catch it, and a release host mid-build must not be left holding half a replaced pair. `cixctl signing-keys set --key=PATH --cert=PATH` takes paths, not PEM text, so a private key never enters shell history or the process list; the dashboard's Host → Signing Keys tab is the paste box. **Verified discriminating** by deleting the mismatch check and confirming two assertions fail. Accepted knowingly: on a host with `https_enabled:false` and no auth the pasted key crosses the management LAN in clear text — recorded in the ADR rather than left implicit.
- **Upgrading a package silently deletes other packages' files (#175, found the hard way).** `libc-dev 2.36-3` staged `cp -a /usr/include/.` — the whole tree — so its manifest claimed files belonging to packages it had nothing to do with. Upgrading it to the decontaminated `2.36-8` unlinked that manifest and took **208 files across 7 other installed packages** with it: all 133 openssl headers, 59 bash headers, `zlib.h`, `uuid.h`, `curses.h`, `libtcc.h`, `FlexLexer.h`. Every one of those packages still reported `installed` with a complete file list; the registry said fine and the rootfs disagreed. It surfaced three steps away, as `build environment: copying usr/include/bash/variables.h from bash@5.2.37-2 failed` during an **elfutils** build. Nothing anywhere checks whether a path one package claims is already claimed by another. **Repairing it exposed a second trap:** delete-then-reinstall does nothing, because an image version is a hash of its package *manifest* (ADR-0155) — removing and re-adding the same package returns the manifest to its previous value, so `image_produce_new_version()` dedups and repoints at the pre-existing *damaged* directory, discarding the freshly extracted tree. The repair has to make the resulting manifest genuinely novel; installing `make` (already in `iso-builder`'s own manifest, just never installed) served, and the fix was confirmed by elfutils then composing and building.
- **`libc-dev` could not be built at all under composed environments, and `kernel-builder` could not be composed because of it.** Two of its 19 pins named versions absent from the artifact cache. `libc-dev 2.36-6` was declared but never built: its build container has no glibc headers, and *both* halves of the recipe read them — what used to supply them was the shared sandbox holding the build host's entire `/usr`, the very thing #168 removed. It now names its own predecessor as a build input (ordinary toolchain bootstrapping, and strictly better than "whatever a long-lived sandbox accumulated" — the input is a checksummed, versioned artifact). That exposed a second fault underneath: every source path read `/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu` while the recipe *stages* the archives to `/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu`, so against a real package input the crt objects resolved and every archive did not. It only ever worked because Debian's merged `/usr` makes both spellings the same file — the same class CLAUDE.md already records for mkbootroot's staging paths. Result: **1,424 files with zero foreign headers**, against 6,123 before, closing #169's package half. `elfutils 0.192-9` and `kmod 34.2-3` declare their build tools for the first time (0.192-8 and 34.2-2 declared none, so they failed before fetching a byte). kmod is a reminder that an artifact in the cache does not save a recipe that cannot build: without `pkg_artifact_sha256` the cache tier is never consulted at all.
- **ADR-0207 phase 4: 192.168.15.95's image store now runs on btrfs, and the snapshot claim is measured rather than asserted.** 41 image versions occupy **8.03 GB of real disk for 29.21 GB of apparent content** — a 3.6× sharing ratio, which is copy-on-write extent sharing and nothing else. On ext4 those same versions each cost their full size; that is why 64 of them had filled a disk earlier the same day. Getting there took three real bugs out of hiding, none of which could be seen before the ones underneath them were fixed.
- **btrfs formatting had never worked on any disk that already had a filesystem — which is every real case (the phase 4 blocker).** `diskformat.c` passed no force flag to `mkfs.btrfs`, on an explicit comment asserting *"mkfs.btrfs takes no -F flag of its own — it always overwrites an existing signature without prompting"*. That is wrong: btrfs-progs uses lowercase `-f`, its own option table reads `OPTLINE("-f, --force", "force overwrite of existing filesystem")`, and `test_dev_for_mkfs(file, force_overwrite)` refuses outright when a filesystem is present. Every attempt on `.95` failed, which is why `sda` was formatted ext4 in the first place.
- **It was invisible because the format never captured what mkfs said** — `"mkfs.btrfs failed"` and nothing else. That is the **fourth** instance of this exact gap (#125, #132, the artifact-export stderr fix, mkinstalleriso's), so it is closed the same way: the child's output is captured and folded into the error `GET /disks/{name}/format` returns. The first capture still failed to say anything useful — it reported `See https://btrfs.readthedocs.io for more information.`, the *footer* — because "last line" is the wrong heuristic for a tool that prints a documentation link after its errors. Line selection now prefers the last `ERROR` line.
- **A disk converted ext4 → btrfs reported as ext4 forever after.** `mkfs.btrfs` does not zero the ext4 superblock at offset 1024, and `disk_probe_fs_type()` tested ext4 first, so the stale signature won. Confirmed live: `sda`, freshly and successfully formatted, reported `fs_type: "ext4"` from `GET /disks` while `diskrole`'s persisted value — written by the format that had just succeeded — correctly said `btrfs`. Two sources of truth disagreeing, with the operator-facing one wrong, on precisely the migration path this ADR is about. btrfs's magic at `0x10040` is outside anything ext4 writes, so it is now tested first.
- **`btrfs-progs` is packaged (7.1-5), which is what put `mkfs.btrfs` on a Cix host at all.** mkbootroot stages it only when `cix-hosttools` carries one, and the recipe declared no build tools so it could not be built (#168) — nor could `libblkid` beneath it. The recipe was already right about the important part: `--disable-libudev` means our `mkfs.btrfs` needs only `libuuid`/`libblkid`/`libz`/`libc`, all already staged, which also removes libudev from the installer ISO's closure where it existed only for Debian's build. Three TCC gaps en route: no `-MM`, no `__SIZEOF_LONG__`, and no `__thread` — the last being the same limitation `elfutils` already forces gcc for.
- **The storage migration ran for real, both ways.** `rebuildable-storage` moved to the OS disk and back onto the freshly-made btrfs `sda` — the first successful use of the path #172 established had *never* worked (its destination root was never created). 405 recipes and their 117 artifact approvals survived both moves intact.
- **The ISO toolchain builds, and a deleted `.pc` file was why it could not (#174).** `sbsigntools` failed at `configure: error: libcrypto (from the OpenSSL package) is required` while the headers and `libcrypto.so` were both present and correct — its `configure.ac` finds libcrypto **only** through `PKG_CHECK_MODULES`, and `openssl` 3.0.20 deleted its whole pkgconfig directory under a comment asserting *"nothing here ... uses pkg-config"*. The premise expired the moment a consumer arrived, and the error named OpenSSL while OpenSSL looked fine. `openssl` **3.0.20-2** fixes it without patching anything: an **absolute** `--libdir=/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu` leaves OpenSSL's own `LIBDIR` empty, so its Makefile template takes the branch that emits `libdir=` verbatim and generates a truthful `.pc` on its own — verified by generating the Makefile both ways (default → `LIBDIR=lib64`; absolute → `libdir=/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu`). The libraries are now *installed* where this project keeps them instead of installed elsewhere and hand-moved, so 3.0.20's four-file `mv` is gone and there is no second, hand-maintained statement of where they live. Its `pkg_build_depends` was read off the **generated Makefile**, not copied from a similar recipe: `cmp` appears 2149 times (one per object's dependency rule), so `diffutils` is load-bearing and copying grub's list would have failed the build — while `sed`/`grep`/`find`/`xargs` occur only in `clean`, the FIPS target and a maintainer target, and are correctly absent. `perl` drops out of `pkg_depends` because since ADR-0199 `pkg_build_depends` is what expresses a build-time need, and naming it in both dragged a full perl into every image installing openssl.
- **`sbsigntools` 0.9.5-9: TCC rejects GCC's double-dash `--std=`.** With libcrypto found, the build died on every file in `src/` with `tcc: error: invalid option -- '--std=gnu99'` — upstream's `AM_CFLAGS` uses the two-dash spelling GCC accepts as a synonym. Probed directly to find the exact boundary rather than inferring it: `--std=gnu99` fails, `-std=gnu99` is accepted, and `-Wall`/`-Wextra`/`-Werror` all pass through fine, so one spelling is the entire incompatibility. Fixed with a thin `CC` wrapper (the `toolwrap` pattern `chrony`/`procps` already use) that rewrites `--std=X` to `-std=X` and carries the `-D__STDC_NO_VLA__=1` regex fix alongside it. Overriding `AM_CFLAGS` on the make command line was considered and rejected: a command-line variable beats every makefile assignment including the `AM_CFLAGS += -DOPENSSL_API_COMPAT=...` that `src/Makefile.am` adds under `if HAVE_OPENSSL3`, so the override would have had to restate upstream's own conditional flag logic inside our recipe.
- **`isotools` 2.14-2 stages a *measured* library closure; 2.14's was read off the contaminated sandbox.** It copied `liblzma.so.5.4.1`, `libbz2.so.1.0.4` and `libz.so.1.2.13` out of `/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu` — those exact minor-version filenames are Debian's, and no package in this recipe set installs any of them, so they can only have come from the pre-ADR-0199 shared sandbox seeded with the build host's entire `/usr` (#168). Against a real composed image those `cp` calls name files that do not exist, so this recipe could not have built since that sandbox was retired. The new closure is `readelf -d` on each published artifact followed to a fixed point: `grub-mkrescue`, `mtools` → `libc.so.6`; `xorriso` → `libz.so.1`; `sbsign`/`sbverify` → `libcrypto.so.3`; then `libcrypto.so.3` and `libz.so.1.3.2` → `libc.so.6` only (glibc 2.36 folded `libdl` into libc, so openssl's `-ldl -pthread` adds no `DT_NEEDED`). **`sbsign` links libcrypto and not libuuid**, which is not the obvious reading of `configure.ac` — that file does check for libuuid, but `src/Makefile.am` adds `$(uuid_LIBS)` only to `sbvarsign`/`sbsiglist`/`sbkeysync`, none of which this artifact harvests. Source paths mattered as much as the file list: zlib installs to `/usr/lib`, not the `/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu` 2.14 looked in. `mkinstalleriso.c`'s comment naming the removed libraries was corrected in the same change.
- **Phase 1 (#158) — image store.** A btrfs-primitives module in the runtime lib (`src/btrfs.c`: subvolume create / snapshot / destroy / qgroup-EXCL quota, each with a non-btrfs fallback, since ext4 retires only in phase 4 and the btrfs-incapable dev sandbox keeps the suite running forever). `image_create`/`image_delete`/`image_produce_new_version` are subvolume-aware: a version is created as a subvolume, produced forward as an **O(1) writable snapshot** instead of a hardlink copy, and destroyed as one. The ext4 paths are byte-identical to before — proven by the suite, which runs them.
- **Phase 2 (#159) — container rootfs.** On btrfs a container's rootfs is a writable snapshot of its image's subvolume, self-bound and pivoted into **with no overlay** — the machinery generalizes the userns direct-pivot path ADR-0179 already built. The on-disk presence of `<base>/rootfs` is the storage-mode marker (the filesystem is the one source of truth; revival keys off it, so a restart can never silently re-provision away a container's writes). Quota moves to qgroups in **exclusive** bytes — a snapshot references its whole image from the first instant, and the quota owed is the container's own divergence. File staging, stopped-container file access, disk-usage reporting and deletion all follow the marker; cross-disk storage migration of snapshot containers is refused loudly until phase 4's tooling. A copy-based `--test-direct-rootfs` mode gives the sandbox full coverage of everything but the snapshot ioctl itself.
- **Overlay's code retirement moved from phase 2 to phase 4, for measured reasons** recorded as a dated correction in the ADR: the sandbox cannot host btrfs at all, the staged test toolchain is ~1GB and `test_pkg` creates a build container per install — a full-copy fallback means 15–25GB of copying per suite run — and hardlinks are unsafe for a writable rootfs. Overlay remains the non-btrfs path (what every unmigrated ext4 host actually runs) and dies together with ext4.
- **Phase 3 (#160) — user namespaces by default, opt-out.** A container created without an explicit `userns` field now takes the platform default (`daemon-config.userns_default`, **on** for fresh installs — the secure-by-default posture the owner set); an explicit true/false always wins, and the platform sets `userns:false` on its own build containers, stated in code rather than inherited from a memset. **The resolved mode is pinned into the persisted definition at creation, image_version-style** — without the pin, flipping the platform default would have silently swapped every pre-existing container's isolation mode (and storage layout) on its next restart; the regression test flips the default while a container is stopped and proves revival stays pinned. On btrfs a userns container's rootfs is the same O(1) snapshot a non-userns one gets — host-0-owned, extent sharing intact — presented through `MOUNT_ATTR_IDMAP` applied by the parent on the fork-shared detached fd between map-write and child-release (no fd passing, no per-inode chown); volumes get the same id-mapped treatment, closing ADR-0179's EOVERFLOW gap. Non-btrfs hosts keep the live-proven phase-2b copy+chown path; revival reads which presentation a rootfs needs from its own ownership. The dev sandbox's LSM forbids `uid_map` writes outright, so the fixture seeds `userns_default:false` through the ordinary config channel and the kernel-side proof belongs to `.95`. The `userns` API contract — which had zero `openapi.yaml` coverage since ADR-0179 — is documented in both contract files.
- **Upgrade migration: a definition persisted before the default flip is pinned to `userns:false` at load** (`migrate_pin_userns_absent()`, same one-shot shape as issue #76's `ldap_login` migration). Post-flip creates always carry the pin, so an absent key means the def predates the flip — and non-userns is the mode it actually ran with. Without this, `.95`'s existing containers would flap to userns on their first post-upgrade revival. The regression test strips the pin from the persisted file between daemon restarts, sets the default to true, and proves revival stays non-userns (bug reintroduced under full rebuild to prove the test catches it).
- **`libc-dev` stages what a libc development environment *is*, by name (2.36-6, closes #169).** It used to run `cp -a /usr/include/.` — the build container's entire include tree, which via the bootstrap is the build *host's* — so every image installing it received another OS's headers: valgrind, Erlang, the host gcc's C++ headers. Now it copies 106 named glibc headers, glibc's own directories, the kernel UAPI trees, and the multiarch entries **named individually** (that directory also holds libstdc++, libffi, lua and openssl headers, so wholesale copying is precisely how contamination got in). Result: **1,405 files / 11 MB, down from 6,128 / 99.8 MB**, with real Cix sources still compiling against it. A build-time gate now fails the recipe if any known-foreign tree appears, so a regression shows up as a failed build rather than a shipped artifact — and that gate immediately caught a bug in my own allowlist: top-level `sys/` on this host is libcap-dev's, not glibc's, so it is now staged only when it genuinely contains glibc's `sys/types.h`.
- **Two structural contamination paths found and filed (#168, #169), and the `kernel-builder` artifact withdrawn because of them.** `cix-builder` *is* the shared build sandbox (`PKG_BUILD_SANDBOX_IMAGE`), `pkg bootstrap` copies the host's whole `/usr` into it, and every successful install folds into it forever — so it held ~8 GB / 88,798 entries of a developer workstation (rustup, cargo, chromium, node, go, qemu, sudo, several gcc trees), **93% belonging to no package in its manifest**. Separately, `libc-dev.recipe` does `cp -a /usr/include/.`, carrying the build container's entire `/usr/include` — Debian's Erlang, valgrind and gcc-12 C++ headers — into *any* image that installs it. The image artifact published today was built on a Cix host but contained those foreign headers, so it was withdrawn from the cache and its checksum removed from the recipe: built-on-Cix is only half the rule.
- **`kernel-builder` built on 192.168.15.95** (artifact withdrawn pending #169). 19 packages including a Cix-built `gcc 16.2.0-11` pulled from the artifact cache, and `kmod` — whose absence from `dev` was half the reason the documented self-hosted kernel build could never have worked. Two packages (`bzip2`, `m4`) arrived as genuine transitive dependencies and are now named in the manifest, because an image's version *is* the hash of that list: a manifest short of reality computes an artifact URL that does not resolve.
- **`elfutils` stops guessing which gcc it is patching (0.192-8).** Its `pkg_build()` wrote a `syslimits.h` correction to a hardcoded `.../12.5.0/include-fixed/` path — the gcc present when the fix was written — so any image with a different gcc failed with a bare "No such file or directory" naming a path nobody had thought about since. It now asks gcc its version, and says so in a sentence when there is no gcc at all. The correction itself is unchanged and still needed.
- **Every build image now has one job (ADR-0208).** These manifests were never designed — each recipe says so in its own header (*"Captured from 192.168.15.95"*), so a package list was whatever a box happened to hold when it was snapshotted. That is how `cix-builder`, the image that exists to build TCC-only code, came to carry `gcc:9.5.0-6`: nobody chose it, a capture took it. It is not inert either — an available gcc is exactly how a `configure` without an explicit `CC=tcc` silently picks the wrong compiler, which is how an `sshd` once shipped with `-lpam` on its link line and no PAM in the resulting ELF. `cix-builder` 3.0.0 drops gcc and pins the patched `tcc 0.9.27-9`. New `kernel-builder` holds the real GCC toolchain plus `kmod`/`bc`/`bison`/`flex`/`elfutils` the kernel genuinely needs — it is the **one** image legitimately holding gcc. `dev` is renamed `iso-builder`, with `grub`/`sbsigntools`/`xorriso`/`mtools` in its manifest rather than installed by hand afterwards: "dev" named no job, so it got prescribed for kernel builds it could not perform, and an image called "iso-builder" without the ISO tools would not be one. Every operator-facing reference moved with the rename; the ADRs and ROADMAP keep their historical text.
- **Build environments are composed, never inherited (ADR-0209, ADR-0210, closes the mechanism half of #168).** Four things went at once, because each depended on the others. A recipe that declares no build tools now **fails**, naming itself — there is no fallback environment, so a build can never quietly run against something fuller than it asked for. Nothing folds into a shared sandbox any more: `cix-builder` stops being the accumulating union of everything ever installed on a host. `pkg bootstrap`'s live host-`/usr` copy is refused permanently — not narrowed, because copying another operating system's files is the wrong thing, not the amount. And a composed environment is destroyed when its build ends, so `__buildenv-*` images stop piling up; it is kept only while a `keep_on_failure` container still needs it as its lowerdir, which the suite caught me getting wrong.
- **`base` stops being privileged (ADR-0210)** and the baseline shrinks to the glibc floor — `libtinfo` and `libgcc_s` are ncurses and gcc, packages we build ourselves and were pointlessly copying Debian's versions of. What remains is named in the code as the last unclosed link in the bootstrap rather than left implicit.
- **The default image is created by the daemon, and now actually exists (ADR-0210).** `cix-install` copied a C runtime into `images/base/rootfs`, and `mkinstalleriso` staged a `payload/cix-runtime` tree on every ISO to supply it, on the stated grounds that nothing else ever would. That path stopped being read when ADR-0107/0108 made images versioned — container creation resolves strictly through `image_current_version()` — so the seeding wrote to a directory nothing consults. Removing it exposed the bug it was masking: a fresh daemon reported `{"images":[]}` and refused a container on `base` with `"image rootfs does not exist"`, because nothing created the default image except a first `pkg install` doing it as a side effect. **A freshly installed box could not create a container at all.** `ensure_default_image()` now materializes it at boot from an empty manifest through the same `image_create()` every other image uses, idempotent by construction. Verified live before and after against a fresh data directory (`{"images":[]}` and a refusal, then `base` present at the empty manifest's own hash with a container actually running on it), and end to end by `test_installer` — a real install plus two independent QEMU boots, its assertions rewritten to prove the *replacement* works rather than deleted, scanning for the version directory instead of hardcoding a hash that would fail for the wrong reason later.
- **A storage migration would have silently gutted every image, and its failures were undiagnosable (#172).** Moving a real host's 15 GB image store onto a second disk failed twice with `bulk copy failed` and *nothing whatsoever in the log store* — the copy runs in a forked child whose stderr nothing captured, so the reason died with it. That is the #125/#132 pattern again, on an operation that moves a host's entire image and package store. `storagemigrate` now pipes `treecopy_last_error()` out of the child, and every `treecopy` failure names its operation and path (`mkdir: /x/usr: No such file or directory`) instead of returning a bare `-1`. **The worse half was hidden behind it:** `treecopy` skipped device nodes *silently*, justified by a comment asserting they are "never expected under any of this project's own storage-placement trees" — true for state- and log-storage, false for the image store, which is exactly what this endpoint moves. `pkg_seed_image_baseline()` stages `/dev/null`, `/dev/zero`, `/dev/full` and `/dev/ptmx` into every image rootfs (ADR-0150 added ptmx so `posix_openpt()` works), so a migration that *succeeded* would have produced an image store whose containers fail on `/dev/null` and cannot allocate a PTY — surfacing days later, nowhere near the cause. The comment was not merely wrong, it was load-bearing: it justified skipping silently rather than failing. Device nodes and fifos are now copied with `mknod`, anything else fails loudly, and the **mode is preserved explicitly** because `mknod()` applies the umask — a 0666 `/dev/null` lands at 0644, unwritable by any container not running as host root, which is the default since ADR-0207 phase 3 (verified source 666 → copy 666; without the fix, 644). `test_treecopy` covers both halves and was confirmed to catch the original bug by restoring the silent skip.
- **Image versions can be reclaimed, and until now they could not (`POST /v1/images/gc`, ADR-0209).** Every install produces a new immutable version (ADR-0107/0108), a container pins whichever was current when it was created, and *nothing anywhere in the API ever removed one*. Not theoretical: 66 versions of an 8 GB rootfs filled a 16 GiB partition, and the disk filling up is how it was found. A version is kept if it is its image's `current_version`, if a live container pins it, or if a stored container definition names it — that third source is the one easy to miss, because a stopped container has no registry entry at all and collecting its version would leave it permanently unable to start. Refused with `409` while a package job is in flight (a build holds its image rootfs as its container's lowerdir). Versions are enumerated from the **filesystem**, not the recorded history: `IMAGE_MAX_VERSION_HISTORY` caps the list at 256 while `image_record_version()` keeps repointing past it, so a long-lived image can own directories its own history no longer names — precisely the ones most worth reclaiming. `cixctl image gc [--dry-run]` and Preview/Reclaim buttons on the dashboard's Images page complete the three surfaces. **Verified with the discriminating case:** a container pinned to a deliberately *non-current* version protects it, and deleting that container makes the same version collectable — a test pinning only the current version would pass with the reference scan deleted outright, confirmed by deleting it (three assertions fail). `apparent_bytes` is named as such everywhere because on btrfs a version is a snapshot sharing extents, so real reclaimed space is usually well below it.
- **Whole-rootfs image artifacts are dropped; package artifacts are the only published binaries (ADR-0209).** ADR-0123's fast path let a fully-`pinned` image recipe carrying an `image_artifact_sha256=` be applied by fetching one tarball and extracting it as the image's entire rootfs, skipping every per-package build. That is the mechanism that took one contaminated capture and shipped it to every host (#168), and it was a second representation of something a package set plus a manifest already describes completely. The whole tier goes: the fetch, the async job, `POST /v1/images/{name}/apply-recipe`'s 202 branch, `GET /v1/images/recipe-apply-status` and its schema, the `cixctl image recipe-apply-status` command, the dashboard's Apply-status panel, and the `image_artifact_sha256=` field itself — no longer parsed, and removed from the five recipes that still declared one. Applying a recipe is now bulk-declare and nothing else, always `204`. **The test was inverted rather than deleted:** it still builds a real, correctly-named, correctly-checksummed artifact and serves it from a real HTTP server with the artifact config pointed at it, then proves none of that matters — asserting *absence* on disk, because an artifact quietly fetched anyway would still return 204. Confirmed discriminating by planting the payload where a fetch would have put it and watching the assertion fail.
- **The package test suite bootstraps the way a real host does.** No fabricated toolchain: real recipe-built artifacts are seeded into each test daemon's own cache and install as cache hits, needing no build environment at all — with every artifact verified against the checksum in its own recipe, and both refusal paths (tampered bytes, missing bytes) proven rather than assumed.
- **TCC learns `__has_include` (tcc 0.9.27-9).** Upstream 0.9.27 implements none of the `__has_*` operators, and in a preprocessor conditional an unknown identifier evaluates to 0 — so a real `#if __has_include(<stdcountof.h>)` became `0(<stdcountof.h>)`, a call through a non-function, and the translation unit died with `function pointer expected` pointing at a blank line. Not theoretical: util-linux 2.42's `include/c.h` uses it, so **libblkid could not be compiled at all** — and libblkid is what `btrfs-progs` needs, which provides the `mkfs.btrfs` that ADR-0207 makes the platform's storage depend on. Only `__has_include` is added, deliberately: its siblings (`__has_attribute`/`__has_feature`/`__has_extension`) need no compiler support because portable code defines its own fallback for them — util-linux does exactly that a few lines above the line that broke — while `__has_include` is the one that cannot be faked, since any fallback would have to answer the question it asks. Resolution walks the same search list in the same order as a real `#include`, testing only openability. **Proven sufficient, not just necessary:** libblkid now configures and builds end to end with the patched compiler, producing a real 3.2 MB `libblkid.so.1.1.0` exporting 647 symbols — so `__has_include` was the only gap behind it, not merely the first. The patch is applied with `sed` and a heredoc, not `python3`: a composed build environment contains only the recipe's *declared* build tools, and `-8` (which used python) died on the box with `python3: command not found` before compiling a line — recipe versions are immutable once published, so the correction is `-9` rather than an edit. The recipe carries a build-time gate asserting all three answers (existing header present, nonexistent absent, nonexistent quoted absent), matching the do-while gate `-7` already established.
- **Compressed archives no longer need a shell — the real cause of every failed export on an installed host (#164).** GNU tar spawns `--use-compress-program=` through `/bin/sh`, and the Cix control-plane root deliberately has none: nothing in `cixd` uses `popen`/`system`, every subprocess is an explicit absolute-path `execve`. The shell's failed exec was reported by tar against the *compress program*, so it surfaced as `/usr/bin/gzip: Cannot exec: No such file or directory` on a host where gzip was present and ran fine — confirmed by pulling that exact binary off `.95` (ordinary ELF, needs only the staged loader and libc) and by reproducing the failure in a locally-built control-plane root, where adding a shell fixes it. Decompression was never affected (tar handles `-xzf`/`-xf` itself), which is why installs worked while **every** image/artifact export and **every** `pkg_cache_save()` failed silently on every real host. New `daemon/src/targz.c` builds the pipeline directly — `tar -cf -` into a pipe `gzip -c` reads, both exec'd by absolute path — with no shell and no temporary uncompressed copy (an image export is gigabytes; a plain `.tar` first would double peak disk on the partition being exported). Output is byte-identical to before, asserted in the test, so published artifacts stay valid; the `tar`/`gzip` paths now live in one header instead of three places. This also completes issue #125, whose fix removed the bare-`gzip` PATH lookup but left the shell in the path. `test_targz` stages a root with no `/bin/sh` and archives from inside it — a plain call would have passed against the broken code — verified by reintroducing the bug under a full rebuild.
- **Kernel build guide corrected.** It still told operators to run `python3 -m http.server 8901` before a self-hosted kernel build — a step that predates the recipe being pinned to a real Gitea raw URL for its config fragment, and that today serves a port nothing reads. Removed, with a note saying why so nobody reinstates it. The same section now states plainly that `recipes/image/dev` carries neither `gcc` nor `kmod`, so the `--build-image=dev` it used to prescribe cannot actually build a kernel as-published — found while investigating why 192.168.15.95 had no image able to build one.
- **A host missing `mkfs.btrfs` now says so.** `diskformat.c`'s child wrapper collapsed the `mkfs` process's own exit 127 into 1, which made `diskformat_completed()`'s 127 branch — the one message that names the cause, "the control-plane image was built without it" — unreachable for exactly the case it was written for. Confirmed live: a real `fs_type:"btrfs"` format against a control-plane image built without `btrfs-progs` reported the useless "mkfs.btrfs failed" while the specific message sat there dead. The exit code is now propagated. Not covered by a test — this sandbox has no block devices to format at all (the same constraint `test_storage_placement` already documents), so this is a reasoned fix against live evidence, not a test-proven one.
- **Image/artifact export failures now carry the tar child's actual stderr** (`g_artifact_export_errfd`, drained bounded at completion) — found live on `.95` during phase 4: every export failed as bare `tar failed (status 0x200)` with the real complaint written to a stderr nothing captured, the same diagnostic-gap class issues #125/#132 document. The status line and log entry now append the child's own words.
- **Phase 4 (#161), first slice — btrfs becomes the install default.** `cix-install` formats `cix-containers` btrfs (full label now, no ext4 16-char truncation) and `cix-config` btrfs `--mixed` (64MiB is below the separate-profile minimum; mixed block groups are btrfs-progs' documented answer for tiny filesystems). No mkfs-time quota flags — btrfs quota is qgroups, enabled at runtime per container. The installer ISO stages `mkfs.btrfs` (+`libudev`); `mkfs.ext4` stays staged through the transition. Boot (`boot_init`) and `cix-recover` mount the platform partitions btrfs-then-ext4 — a not-yet-migrated ext4 box boots the new build unchanged, and the ext4 branch retires with the rest of ext4 once btrfs has run production. `test_installer` inspection reworked from `debugfs`/`e2fsck` (ext4-only) to `btrfs restore`; the debugfs `-w` marker-injection persistence proof — impossible offline on btrfs — is replaced by the stronger-in-substance check that installer-seeded content survives two real, independent QEMU boots byte-identical and cixd's grouped layout is present on the raw partition afterwards. Partition *resize* remains ext4-only (`resize2fs`) — filed as #163, not a migration blocker.
- **Two pre-existing lifecycle bugs found by the new test's 200ms stop/start cadence, both fixed:** `POST /start` during an in-flight stop returned the idempotent 200 for the *dying* incarnation — acking a start that never happened, leaving the container down while the caller believes it restarted (every restart script had this window; it now returns a retryable 409). And the stop/delete async completion removed its registry entry **by name**, so a same-name container registered in the completion window would be removed — and killed — by its predecessor's teardown (now guarded by incarnation identity: captured pid + started_at). A third gap — the files API on a cleanly stopped container is a race, then a 404, while an *exited* container's files stay accessible indefinitely — is pre-existing, orthogonal, and filed as #162 rather than smuggled into this change.

### Part 210 (in progress): what a real deploy finds that review does not

Five releases went to 192.168.15.95 in one afternoon (v2.1.1 → v2.1.5). Every one of them found something, and **three of the bugs were introduced by fixes made earlier the same day** — which is the substantive finding: on this platform a fix is a hypothesis until a real box runs it.

- **A good update could silently revert two reboots later.** `confirm_boot()` took whichever entry `readdir()` returned first, so with both `cix-a.conf` and `cix-a+3.conf` on the ESP it could "confirm" the already-confirmed one and no-op — leaving the real counter ticking down until systemd-boot gave up on the new slot. The update booted, ran, passed every health check, and was undone anyway. Caught on the real host after a successful cutover. Selection moved into `esp.c` as a rank rather than a first match.
- **The ESP ordering model was wrong, and confidently so.** `will boot:` ignored `sort-key`/`version` and sorted ids ascending, reporting that a correctly staged update would never boot. That answer was nearly acted on — and the obvious response (pinning `default` to one slot) genuinely breaks the *next* update. Settled by extracting a real `bootctl` and asking it. Issue #147, filed on the strength of the wrong model, is closed as invalid.
- **Boot slots can be switched now (#154, `GET/POST/DELETE /system/boot-next`).** Rollback previously meant waiting three reboots for a counter to exhaust, or reinstalling. Uses systemd-boot's `LoaderEntryOneShot`: one boot, then normal selection resumes, so a machine that fails to come back is never left pinned to a broken slot. A slot with no loader entry is refused rather than armed — arming a boot into nothing needs a console to recover from, which is the situation the feature exists to avoid.
- **A fresh install can deploy to itself (#146).** `mkbootroot` fell back to a `/usr/bin/mksquashfs` that exists only on a dev box. The first fix staged it from the bare host — so it worked only where it was not needed, and reproduced the original failure on the real box. Correct source is `cix-hosttools`.
- **A cache-hit hostbuild ran none of the work that follows a build (#144).** The fast path duplicated the post-build follow-up and omitted the bootroot assembly, so `--deploy` reported success and produced no image at all. One `pkg_completion_followup()` now serves both paths.
- **Provisioning became an endpoint (ADR-0205).** `cixctl dns provision` sequenced four REST calls itself — a CLI feature with no endpoint behind it, which the mandate forbids and which would have forced the dashboard to write the same sequence again. Required splitting `handle_create()` so a workflow endpoint creates containers through the same implementation as `POST /containers`.
- **DNS forwarders, provisioning and the ESP reached the dashboard**, and `cixctl update` gained `--image-url=`. Every capability the CLI could reach and the web could not was half-delivered.
- **Two test-methodology corrections**, both found by deliberately reintroducing a bug to check the test caught it. The first `confirm_boot` regression test **passed against the broken code**, because `readdir` order is unspecified and this sandbox returns the opposite order from the real vfat ESP; the decision is now a pure function asserted directly. And `test_dns`/`test_container_restart` leaked host bridges on failure, poisoning the *next* run with cascading errors that read exactly like a code regression — they now enumerate containers rather than naming them.

### Part 209 (in progress): closing the gaps Part 208 could only name

Part 208 ended with a retrospective and eight issues rather than features, because the DNS bring-up had been seven-eighths workaround. This part is the other half: turning those issues into mechanisms. Two of them turned out to be the same shape — a capability that *looked* present, was routed around in practice, and so was never actually exercised.

- **DNS forwarders are configuration now, not argv (#134, [ADR-0203](docs/adr/0203-dns-forwarders-are-daemon-owned-config.md)).** `GET/PUT /v1/dns/forwarders`, persisted with the rest of host config and applied live to every registered server via a daemon-written servers-file plus `SIGHUP`. The old convention — `--server=1.1.1.1` baked into each DNS container's command line — cost three real things: changing a forwarder meant **recreating core infrastructure**, `dns-1` and `dns-2` could **silently disagree** with nothing tying their argv together, and "what does this platform resolve through?" had **no answer at all**, the value living only inside a running process. One `PUT` now updates every replica, and a newly registered server picks up the current list without being told. `dnsmasq.recipe` and both DNS container recipes move to `--servers-file=`.
- **A host can update itself over its own API (#141, [ADR-0204](docs/adr/0204-the-daemon-fetches-its-own-update-image.md)).** `POST /v1/system/update` accepts `image_url` + a **mandatory** `image_sha256`. The endpoint previously took only `image_path` — a file already on the box — but an installed Cix host has no SSH, no shell, no scp target, and the API's 1 MiB cap rules out sending a ~10 MB squashfs as a body. So **the one endpoint whose entire job is updating the control plane could not be used to update it**, and every deploy in this project's history routed around it instead. The checksum is required rather than optional because this call writes a boot slot: an unverified image surfaces its damage at the next reboot, the worst possible moment. The URL is rewritten into the existing `image_path` flow, so slot-writing — the highest-consequence code here — keeps exactly one path.
- **A cache-hit install no longer demands the build tools it is not going to use (#144).** Installing a package whose artifact is already cached ran the build-container setup anyway, so a missing build tool failed an install that was never going to compile anything. The cache-hit branch now roots directly on the target image and skips container setup entirely.
- **Documentation swept for the drift that made Part 208 expensive.** `/dns/forwarders` was in the API README but had **never reached `openapi.yaml`** — precisely the divergence the Documentation Map exists to prevent, found by auditing rather than by it biting. Fixed, along with the README's three now-superseded `--server=` passages, the missing `image_url` contract in both files, four ADRs absent from the ADR index (0201–0204), and six broken intra-document anchors.
- **15 package artifacts rebuilt and re-approved (#130/#139).** Their cached artifacts had been published through `GET /containers/{name}/files`, which returns file **content with no mode** — so every binary inside arrived non-executable, checksummed perfectly, and died at `execve` with nothing naming the artifact as the cause.
